explain.say: Lightning strikes a car, and the people inside usually walk away unharmed. Why? A metal shell keeps the electric field out of its inside. Carl Friedrich Gauss gave us the law that explains it. On the board: a metal shell carrying 1 nanocoulomb of charge, wrapped in an imaginary bubble we choose ourselves, called a Gaussian surface.

explain.say: Start with the outer bubble. Picture field lines streaming out of the charge and poking through its skin. The total field passing out through a surface is called electric flux. Gauss's law says the flux out of any closed surface equals the charge inside, divided by epsilon nought, the permittivity of free space. Does the size of the bubble matter?

explain.say: Not at all! For 1 nanocoulomb inside, the flux is about 113 units whether the bubble is the size of a pea or a planet. A bigger bubble has more area, but the field on it is weaker by exactly the same factor. So what is the flux through a bubble with no charge inside?

explain.say: Zero. Now put it to work. By symmetry, E is the same all over a sphere, so E times 4 pi r squared equals Q over epsilon nought. Outside the shell that gives the familiar k Q over r squared: 900 newtons per coulomb at the surface and 225 at 20 centimetres. Inside, a bubble encloses no charge, so the field is zero. See the curve leap up at the shell?

curves.label: E of 1 nC shell
curves.ask: Why is the field zero inside a charged metal shell?

draw.text: E·4πr² = Q/ε₀  ⇒  E = kQ/r² outside, 0 inside

explain.say: That jump is the shell itself. The empty inside of a conductor feels no field, which is why a car body or a Faraday cage shields you, and why a microwave oven's metal mesh keeps the waves in. Excellent! Exam tip: choose a Gaussian surface that matches the symmetry: a sphere for a point charge, a cylinder for a long wire, a flat pillbox for a sheet.

faq.a: The total electric flux out of any closed surface equals the charge enclosed divided by epsilon nought. It is one of Maxwell's four equations.
Electric flux measures how much electric field passes through a surface: the field times the area it crosses at right angles, added over the whole surface.
An imaginary closed surface you choose so you can apply Gauss's law. You pick a shape that matches the symmetry, so the field is the same everywhere on it.
asks: How do I choose a Gaussian surface?

faq.q: Why is the field zero inside a charged metal shell?
faq.a: All the charge sits on the outer surface. A Gaussian surface inside encloses no charge, so with the symmetry the field there must be zero.
asks: How does a Faraday cage work?
Why is a car safe in lightning?

faq.q: Does the size of the Gaussian surface change the flux?
faq.a: No. A larger surface has more area but a weaker field, and the two effects cancel exactly. Only the enclosed charge matters.
asks: Does flux depend on the radius?

facts: Carl Friedrich Gauss formulated his law in 1835, though it was published only in 1867, after his death.
The permittivity of free space, epsilon nought, is about 8.85 times 10 to the minus 12 farads per metre.

quiz.say: A closed surface encloses 2 nanocoulombs. What is the electric flux through it? Take epsilon nought as 8.85 times 10 to the minus 12.
quiz.show: A closed surface encloses 2 nC. What is the electric flux through it? (ε₀ ≈ 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m)
quiz.why: Flux is Q over epsilon nought: 2 times 10 to the minus 9, over 8.85 times 10 to the minus 12, is about 226.

wrong.1: That is the flux for 1 nanocoulomb, not 2.
wrong.2: The flux is zero only when no net charge is enclosed.

quiz.say: A charge sits outside a closed surface. What is the net flux through the surface?
quiz.show: A charge sits outside a closed surface. The net flux through the surface is...
quiz.why: Every field line that enters the surface also leaves it, so the net flux is zero.

wrong.1: Flux is positive only when net positive charge is inside.
wrong.2: Flux is negative only when net negative charge is inside.
